raw_graphql_pull_request.body: # SGLang Optimizations for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on H20: 4–10× Faster Long-Input TTFT > Main authors: Hanlin Gao, Wengang Zheng, Yusong Gao, Yun Zhang > > This draft PR is a write-up, not a merge request. The code is the `dsv41-flash-h20` branch of this repository. The changes are meant to go upstream piece by piece. ## Introduction We run an agent workload whose requests average **about 170K input tokens** each, with short outputs. On H20 the first bottleneck for this traffic is prefill. **H20 has about one seventh of the compute of H100, but its NVLink is still 900 GB/s**, so it suits splitting one long request across several GPUs. The branch is based on SGLang upstream main (`5884e4fec6`, October 27, 2026; the same base throughout). It does three things: - **It spreads the prefill of a long input over 8 GPUs.** - **It removes the work that every GPU repeats during decode.** - **It puts every optimization behind one switch.** With the switch off, the code is upstream's, except for the commits that fix upstream bugs. This makes it easy to upstream the changes one at a time. **Results** - **Single node (8×H20-3e):** TTFT on long inputs is **4–10× faster** than upstream main. Decode throughput is **1.9–2.3×** that of upstream main. - **Cold start (8×H20, fresh container):** the time until the server can take requests drops from **31 minutes to 5.3 minutes**. - **Off-peak revenue per GPU-hour:** - On a 34-GPU minimal reproduction demo built from sampled internal business data (2E3P1D, a fixed 3:1 ratio), the two load levels give **¥26.8 (≈$4.0)** at about 50 token/s per user and **¥14.4 (≈$2.2)** at about 100 token/s per user. At the 100 TPS level, P is only about half used. - At our internal system's operating point, 100 token/s per user gives about **¥24.5 (≈$3.7)**. Revenue uses DeepSeek's official off-peak prices. USD figures use the CNY/USD ratio of DeepSeek's own price list (about 6.67). **Code and reproduction** - **Code:** [github.com/antgroup/sglang](https://github.com/antgroup/sglang/tree/dsv41-flash-h20), branch `dsv41-flash-h20` (head `6e6d5d9e13`), which is the head of this PR. - **Model:** [deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017) on Hugging Face. - **Reproducing:** - The single-node numbers can be reproduced with the commands in [Reproduction](#reproduction). - The demo's deployment commands are there too, but the sampled data is not public. - The open-source version cannot connect to Ant Group's internal KV cache system, so the reproduction uses SGLang HiCache L2 in its place. **At a glance: single node vs upstream main** (8×H20-3e, TP8 + prefill CP8 + DSpark) | Metric | Upstream main | This branch | Speedup | |---|---:|---:|---:| | TTFT (cold prefill), 4K input | 0.21 s | 0.09 s | 2.3× | | TTFT (cold prefill), 128K input | 6.9 s | 1.7 s | 4.0× | | TTFT (cold prefill), 512K input | 51.2 s | 7.5 s | 6.9× | | TTFT (cold prefill), 1M input | 163 s | 16.7 s | 9.8× | | Decode throughput, single session | 303 token/s | 583 token/s | 1.9× | | Decode throughput, 64 concurrent | 2.5K token/s | 5.8K token/s | 2.3× | | KV capacity | 20.6M tokens | 27.0M tokens | 1.3× | | Cold start to ready (fresh container, 8×H20 96 GB) | 31 min | 5.3 min | 5.9× | | TTFT of the first 128K request after cold start (same) | 364 s | 1.8 s | — | | GSM8K | 0.922 | 0.915 | — | **At a glance: throughput and revenue** (≈168K average input tokens; revenue per GPU-hour at DeepSeek off-peak prices) | | Output speed per user (p50) | Prefill per GPU (uncached / incl. cache hits) | Decode per GPU | Revenue per GPU-hour | Source | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---| | Demo, 50 TPS level | 51 token/s | 6.8K / 94K token/s | 1.5K token/s | ¥26.8 (≈$4.0) | Measured on the 34-GPU demo | | Demo, 100 TPS level | 95 token/s | 3.6K / 51K token/s | 829 token/s | ¥14.4 (≈$2.2) | Measured on the 34-GPU demo | | Internal system operating point | 100 token/s | 7.4K / 94K token/s | 930 token/s | ¥24.5 (≈$3.7) | Internal system operating point | **Versions** | Item | Value | |---|---| | Model | deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (Hugging Face) | | Baseline | SGLang upstream main, commit `5884e4fec6c0f4453940605896154f5fba4badd9` (merged 2026-10-27 00:07 UTC) | | Baseline image | `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-20261027-5884e4fe` (upstream nightly for that commit) | | This branch | [github.com/antgroup/sglang](https://github.com/antgroup/sglang/tree/dsv41-flash-h20), branch `dsv41-flash-h20` | | Branch head | `6e6d5d9e13915adb01db0856b15d6908eaaa2c48`, 10 commits on top of the baseline | | Scope of changes | Only `python/sglang`, plus tests and docs. Dependencies and sgl-kernel are unchanged, so the branch runs directly in the baseline image | | Measured | 2026-10-27 to 10-29 | | Hardware | Single node: 8×H20-3e (141 GB). Cold start and PD / EPD: 8×H20 (96 GB) nodes | To reproduce, use the upstream baseline image and this branch's code. Inside the image container: ```bash git clone -b dsv41-flash-h20 https://github.com/antgroup/sglang.git && cd sglang && git checkout 6e6d5d9e13 export PYTHONPATH=$PWD/python SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_SM90=1 python3 -m sglang.launch_server ... # full environment variables and arguments in "Reproduction" below ``` ## Results ### Single node: 8×H20-3e vs upstream main Both run TP8 + prefill CP8 + DSpark on the same machine. - The longer the input, the larger the gap: 4× faster at 128K and nearly 10× at 1M. - At 32 and 64 concurrent requests, decode throughput is more than 2.2× that of upstream main. | Metric | Upstream main | This branch | Speedup | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Cold-prefill TTFT, 4K input | 0.211 s | 0.092 s | 2.29× | | Cold-prefill TTFT, 64K input | 2.966 s | 0.857 s | 3.46× | | Cold-prefill TTFT, 128K input | 6.901 s | 1.724 s | 4.00× | | Cold-prefill TTFT, 256K input | 17.681 s | 3.522 s | 5.02× | | Cold-prefill TTFT, 512K input | 51.230 s | 7.476 s | 6.85× | | Cold-prefill TTFT, 1M (1016K) input | 163.386 s | 16.665 s | 9.80× | | Decode throughput, single session (4K in, 1K out) | 303.0 token/s | 583.0 token/s | 1.92× | | Decode throughput, 32 concurrent (total output) | 1982.8 token/s | 4460.7 token/s | 2.25× | | Decode throughput, 64 concurrent (total output) | 2518.1 token/s | 5773.9 token/s | 2.29× | | KV capacity | 20.56M tokens | 26.97M tokens | 1.31× | | Cold start to READY (8×H20 96 GB, fresh container) | 1850 s | 316 s | 5.9× | *Figure 1. This branch vs upstream main on a single node (8×H20-3e, TP8 + prefill CP8 + DSpark). The green numbers on the right are speedups.* ### Cold start: 31 minutes to 5.3 minutes Cold start does not change steady-state performance, but every new instance has to wait through it once. **Setup:** both sides start from a fresh container: the JIT cache is empty and the checkpoint is not in the page cache. **Result on 8×H20 (96 GB):** | | Time to READY | TTFT of the first 128K request after READY | |---|---:|---:| | Upstream main | 1850 s | 364 s | | This branch | 316 s | 1.8 s | *Figure 2. Cold start (8×H20, TP8 + prefill CP8 + DSpark, fresh container, checkpoint not in the page cache).* Upstream main spends its time in two places: - **CUDA graph capture takes 1395 s.** - Almost all of it goes to DeepGEMM precompiling every GEMM shape for every M from 1 to 32768. - After READY, the first 128K request hits two shapes that only appear in long prefills, and each triggers another round of compilation. So its TTFT is six minutes. - **Weight loading takes 340 s**, about 200 s of which is mHC warm-up compilation during loading. This branch changes three things: - It turns off full-M precompilation by default and warms up on sampled shapes. - It ships a JIT manifest with the code. While weights load, 32 processes compile the kernels in the manifest in parallel. - It keeps the page cache instead of dropping it. The result: - Weight loading takes 133 s and CUDA graph capture 86 s. - After READY, no new files appear in the JIT cache directory. - The first 128K request has about the same TTFT as steady state (1.74 s). Note: upstream provides `python3 -m sglang.compile_deep_gemm` to compile DeepGEMM ahead of time, which makes cold start much shorter. This comparison is a plain launch with no preparation. ### Minimal reproduction demo: 2E3P1D on 34 H20 GPUs This demo is a minimal reproduction. It checks the V4.1 PD / EPD path end to end and measures the per-GPU capacity of P and D. It does not represent how the real business is deployed or loaded. - **Traffic:** multi-turn sessions sampled from internal business data, about 47 minutes long, with an average input of about 168K tokens. It is replayed in its original order, with only the arrival rate scaled to the target. - **No comparison:** upstream main does not support EPD for V4.1 yet, so this setup has no upstream baseline. - **Deployment:** 2E3P1D. P uses 3 nodes (24 GPUs), D 1 node (8 GPUs) and E 2 GPUs. - **Load levels:** - At the 50 TPS level, each user gets about 50 token/s. - The 100 TPS level halves the arrival rate. Output speed gets close to 100 token/s, and TTFT is much shorter. | Stage | Metric | 50 TPS | 100 TPS | |---|---|---:|---:| | Prefill | Throughput per GPU (uncached) | 6.8K token/s | 3.6K token/s | | | Throughput per GPU (incl. cache hits) | 94K token/s | 51K token/s | | | Mean input cache hit rate | 92.8% | 93.0% | | | TTFT, mean | 6.2 s | 1.3 s | | | TTFT, p99 | 15.5 s | 9.0 s | | | Mean input length | 168K tokens | 168K tokens | | Decode | Throughput per GPU | 1.5K token/s | 829 token/s | | | Output speed (per user, p50) | 51 token/s | 95 token/s | | Overall | Concurrency (mean requests in flight) | ≈290 | ≈75 | | | Of which decoding | ≈200 | ≈65 | | | Achieved throughput | 13.4 req/s | 7.3 req/s | | | Successful requests | 4000 / 4000 | 4000 / 4000 | | | Off-peak revenue per GPU-hour | ¥26.8 (≈$4.0) | ¥14.4 (≈$2.2) | Notes: - **Prefix cache.** In our internal deployment, P connects to Ant Group's internal KV cache system. The open-source version cannot integrate it, so this setup uses SGLang HiCache L2 instead (host memory, 100 GB per rank); see the launch arguments in [Reproduction](#reproduction). The ≈93% cache hit rate in the table was measured with this configuration. - **Lossy option.** D enables the only lossy option, `fp8_lm_head_target`. - **Concurrency.** It is the number of requests sent but not finished, sampled every 0.5 s while sending, then averaged. "Decoding" means requests that have received their first token and are still generating. - At the 50 TPS level, up to 256 requests decode at once, which is D's limit (`--max-running-requests 256`). - **Throughput per GPU.** It is requests completed per second while sending × mean input (or output) length ÷ number of GPUs. - Throughput including cache hits = uncached throughput ÷ (1 − hit rate). - The cached part needs no recomputation, which is why the two differ by more than 10×. - **Revenue.** It uses DeepSeek's official off-peak prices, shared over all 34 GPUs including E. Per million tokens: - cache-hit input: ¥0.02 ($0.003); - cache-miss input: ¥1 ($0.15); - output: ¥4 ($0.6). - **DSpark.** During the replay, DSpark accepts about 3.6 tokens per step on average. *Figure 3. Key metrics of the demo at its two load levels.* At the 100 TPS level, revenue per GPU is only ¥14.4: - To keep each user at about 100 token/s, D can only output about 829 token/s per GPU. - P runs at only about half its capacity: 3.6K per GPU, against 6.8K at the 50 TPS level. This comes from the fixed 3:1 ratio. Our internal system scales P and D separately with load, so it does not have this limit. ### Internal system operating point vs DeepSeek production Our internal system scales P and D separately with load. At the internal system's operating point, with 100 token/s per user, each GPU processes about 7.4K uncached input tokens/s in prefill and outputs about 930 token/s in decode. At DeepSeek's off-peak prices, that is about ¥24.5 (≈$3.7) per GPU-hour. When DeepSeek released DeepInfer, it published production statistics: - decode runs Wide-EP on 64–128 GPUs; - the KV cache sits on about 100 PiB of 3FS; - the average input is 77K tokens, with a 96% cache hit rate. The GPU model was not disclosed; we assume GB200. In FP8 dense compute per GPU, H20 is about 1/17 of GB200. *Figure 4. Each full bar is DeepSeek production / GB200 (assumed); the filled part is our internal operating point / H20. All per GPU.* | Per GPU | Internal operating point (H20) | DeepSeek production | Ours as a fraction of DeepSeek | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Mean input cache hit rate | ≈92% | 96% | — | | Prefill throughput (incl. cache hits) | 94K token/s | 1.5M token/s | ≈1/16 | | Prefill throughput (uncached) | 7.4K token/s | 60K token/s | ≈1/8 | | Decode throughput | 930 token/s | 14K token/s | ≈1/15 | | Off-peak revenue (per hour) | ¥24.5 (≈$3.7) | ≈¥253 ($38) | ≈1/10 | | Output speed per user | 100 token/s | 230 token/s | ≈1/2.3 | **Note that this comparison is not fair to DeepSeek.** - DeepSeek gives each user 230 token/s; we give 100. - Output speed and per-GPU throughput trade off against each other. In the demo, raising output speed from 51 to 95 cut D's throughput per GPU from 1.5K to 829. DeepSeek reaches its throughput at a much higher output speed. - Their decode runs Wide-EP on 64–128 GPUs, and their KV cache hit rate is also higher. On H20 we really cannot match DeepSeek's output speed, so this comparison only shows orders of magnitude. Our conclusion: for long-input, prefill-heavy workloads on this model, H20 is still usable. Users also accept 50–100 token/s. For reference, on [Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/) (checked October 2026): - [Claude Sonnet 5](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/claude-sonnet-5-high/providers) on Anthropic's official API runs at about 71 token/s; - [Sonnet 5.5](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/claude-sonnet-5-5-high) runs at about 118 token/s. How the figures were derived: - **GB200 FP8 dense compute** is estimated as 720 PFLOPS for a full NVL72 rack (with sparsity) ÷ 72 ÷ 2, which is about 5 PFLOPS. H20 is 296 TFLOPS. - **DeepSeek's $38** is also off-peak, converted with the CNY/USD ratio of the official price list (about 6.67). ### How we measured The single-node numbers were measured on 8×H20-3e (141 GB). Cold start, PD and EPD use 8×H20 (96 GB) nodes. - **TTFT** is cold prefill: no prefix cache hit, 32 output tokens, 1 warm-up run, then the median of 3 runs. - **Decode throughput** uses a fixed 4K input and 1K output. - **Runs:** both sides use the same machine and the same client. Upstream main was measured once; this branch twice, averaged. **Upstream main settings:** - It enables the same TP8, prefill CP8 and DSpark, but not `--enable-decoder-swa-bounded-replay`. With all of these enabled together, upstream crashes on the first request (commit 2 fixes this). - Upstream main also has 14 DSpark / CUDA graph switches that are off by default. Turning all of them on raises its decode throughput by 4–7%. This branch is then still 1.79×, 2.11× and 2.21× of it at single session, 32 concurrent and 64 concurrent. **Cold start method:** - Both sides start from a newly created container with an empty JIT cache. - Before launch, `posix_fadvise(DONTNEED)` evicts the checkpoint from the page cache, and `mincore` confirms that 0% of it is resident. - Timing runs from the launch command to `/health` returning 200. ## One switch: off means upstream The branch adds only three environment variables: | Variable | Effect | |---|---| | `SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_SM90=1` | Enables all optimizations for the deepseek_v41 model on SM90; other models and architectures are unaffected | | `SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_SM90_DISABLE=` | Turns off individual subsystems by name | | `SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_SM90_LOSSY=fp8_lm_head_target` | The only lossy option; must be enabled explicitly | **Subsystems.** The switch covers 14 subsystems: `mhc`, `moe`, `fp8_gemm`, `attn_proj`, `lm_head`, `startup`, `indexer`, `cp`, `prefill_graph`, `decode`, `mix_decode`, `runtime`, `pd`, `epd`. - The switch is parsed once at process start. Each module records the result when it is constructed and never checks again at run time. - A misspelled subsystem name is an error at startup. **Switch off.** With the switch off, the code that runs is upstream's. The exceptions are changes that fix upstream bugs: - Commit 2 is not gated as a whole and can be applied to the baseline on its own. - Ungated fixes and registrations in other commits are listed separately in their commit messages. **Numerics.** Most changes are bit-exact with the kernels they replace. The exceptions, also listed one by one in the commit messages, are: - Following the model's reference implementation, attention output is rounded to FP8 per 32 elements before wo_a. - Some small-M GEMMs use split-K, which changes the FP32 summation order. - mHC uses tf32x3. - Under CP, the MoE reduction sums in FP32 and rounds once. - The decode head swap changes FlashMLA's split. - The prefill indexer scores in FP8; scores match the torch path within tolerance. - When the FlashMLA scheduler picks a non-default split, the output differs from the original by at most 2 bf16 ulp. - The DSpark draft uses an FP8 LM head. All these paths are deterministic: the same input always gives the same output. | # | Commit | Subsystems | Main content | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | feat(dsv41): SM90 optimization switch | — | Switch, subsystem list and docs | | 2 | fix(dsv41): SM90 crash and edge-case fixes | Always on | CP tail-gather crash, top-k overflow, split-K race, etc. | | 3 | perf(dsv41): deterministic SM90 mHC and humming MoE | mhc, moe | Deterministic mHC, Humming W4A8 MoE | | 4 | perf(fp8): SM90 block32 GEMMs, FP8 attention projections and LM head | fp8_gemm, attn_proj, lm_head | FP8 GEMM routing, wo_a and LM head | | 5 | perf(dsv41): fast startup and JIT manifest | startup | Cold start and JIT manifest replay | | 6 | perf(dsv41): SM90 indexer | indexer | Sparse-attention indexer for prefill / decode | | 7 | perf(dsv41): CP prefill | cp, prefill_graph | CP communication, sparse prefill, late-layer skip, prefill graphs | | 8 | perf(dsv41): decode and mix decode TP | decode, mix_decode | FlashMLA scheduling, head swap, TP-SP, DSpark | | 9 | feat(serving): V4.1 serving policies and PD robustness | runtime, pd | Scheduling and cache policies, PD failure handling | | 10 | feat(epd): V4.1 encoder disaggregation | epd | Full V4.1 EPD path | ## Prefill: spreading one long request over 8 GPUs ### CP communication Prefill CP8 interleaves a request's tokens across 8 GPUs. The upstream implementation works, but carries a lot of extra overhead: - every per-layer row exchange goes through NCCL; - the compressor first gathers full hidden rows, then projects all rows on every GPU; - MoE output is all-reduced and then sliced; - under CP each layer also has about 4 ms of host overhead that does not depend on the row count, so for short inputs the host is the bottleneck. All of this communication now goes through NVLink symmetric memory: - **SWA KV and the compressor gathers** are issued by the copy engine before q_b and overlap with compute. - **The compressor** projects only its local rows and then gathers the projected results. The tail compressor goes from a 16384-row GEMM plus one full gather to a 2048-row GEMM plus one output gather. - **MoE.** From 2048 rows per GPU, the copy engine also pulls the MoE inputs. The weighted sum of the routed experts is written straight into each rank's symmetric buffer and then summed in FP32 in rank order. This removes the NCCL all-reduce and the slicing. - **Input embeddings and Engram lookups** are written directly from the shard owner to the target rank in the same way. ### Sparse prefill and late-layer skip **Sparse prefill.** Under CP, upstream sends query rows into the paged decode kernel. We switch back to `flash_mla_sparse_fwd`. On 8×H20, attention time for a cold 128K request drops from 222.8 ms to 199.1 ms. **Bounded replay.** The late-layer skip builds on upstream's bounded replay ([sgl-project/sglang#38798](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38798)). - V4.1 layers 21–39 reuse layer 20's KV, but each layer still has its own 128-token sliding window. - With bounded replay on, layer 20 and later layers compute only the last window of each prefill chunk, and the sliding window is truncated at that window's start. - So bounded replay is an approximation. The upstream docs say it is not numerically equivalent to a full prefill, and recommend turning it off for RL, where logprobs must match the trainer ([V4.1 cookbook](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/5884e4fec6c0f4453940605896154f5fba4badd9/docs/cookbook/autoregressive/DeepSeek/DeepSeek-V4_1.mdx)). - Upstream made it the default without CP in [sgl-project/sglang#44403](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/44403). - The PR's evaluations with it on and off are close: 97.71% for both on AIME 2026 with unlimited output, and 69.03% vs 68.14% on DeepSWE. - The PR also notes that single runs cannot prove accuracy equivalence. - This branch turns it on explicitly under CP8. Commit 2 fixes the crash when these options are combined. See [Accuracy](#accuracy) for the comparison. **Late-layer skip.** It builds on bounded replay. - Suppose that after a chunk, every request still has at least one window left unfilled. That window will be overwritten by a later chunk, so computing it is wasted: nothing reads it. - In that case the whole chunk stops at layer 20 (of 40). Under CP, the row layout that logits and DSpark need is still kept. The result is bit-exact with bounded replay itself. - The scheduler helps guarantee that every late-layer value that is read comes from a full forward pass: - a continuation chunk that falls inside the last window must contain the whole window; - a request that hits the radix cache must re-prefill its last window. ### Prefill CUDA graphs The ≈4 ms per-layer host overhead is removed with CUDA graphs. - **Capture.** Graphs are captured lazily, at the exact local row count, with no padding. A row count is captured the second time it appears. Each segment keeps at most 32 graphs, evicted LRU. - **What stays eager.** The CP KV gather, the indexer and the attention core still run eagerly. - **Failure handling.** After capture, and before the custom all-reduce graph inputs are registered, all ranks vote. If any rank failed to capture, all ranks discard the capture together and fall back to eager. ### Sparse-attention indexer In V4.1's ratio-1/2 layers, an indexer first picks the top-k KV positions for each query, and then sparse attention runs on them. Upstream's prefill indexer is in torch: it dequantizes the index keys to BF16, runs an einsum, then calls `torch.topk`. **Prefill.** - We unpack each request's FP4 keys once, convert them to E4M3 and score them with FP8 tensor cores. - Once the scoring size reaches 2M, H20 switches to a keys-major Gluon kernel. - Top-k uses top-k v2. On ties it always keeps the earlier position, so the result no longer depends on the order of atomics. - Scores match the torch path within tolerance. **Decode and verify.** - FP4 keys are scored straight from the request table. - Several verify rows of the same request share the decoded key tiles. - When there are enough candidate windows, consumer layers score only the candidate blocks instead of scanning the whole context. ### MoE: Humming W4A8 V4.1-Flash stores its routed-expert weights in FP4 (MXFP4), but H20 is a Hopper GPU without FP4 tensor cores. This part uses Humming ([github.com/vllm-project/humming](https://github.com/vllm-project/humming)), **open-sourced by Ant Group**, a JIT-compiled quantized GEMM library. - **How it works.** Humming converts the FP4 weights to FP8 inside the kernel, with the weights' E8M0 scales folded into the operands ahead of time. It then feeds them, together with FP8 activations, into the FP8 tensor cores (W4A8). - **Why it helps.** The weights stay 4-bit in memory, so less data is read, and the compute still runs at FP8 speed. - **Adoption.** SGLang already integrates it as an MoE backend ([sgl-project/sglang#23754](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/23754)). FlashInfer's recent MXFP4×FP8 MoE path for Hopper follows Humming's weight preprocessing and dequantization method (`flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#3738`). Humming is very efficient on H20. We once profiled a cold 128K prefill (TP4 + CP4): - the two routed-expert GEMMs took more than a third of GPU time; - from measured kernel times and shapes, w13 and w2 reached 84% and 83% of FP8 dense peak. This branch changes how Humming is used: - **Stream-K is off.** It accumulates K slices in arrival order, so the first token of a short input could vary from run to run. - **Less padding.** Per-rank weight padding shrinks from 256/128 to 64/64. Under TP8, w13's N drops from 768 to 576. - **Fusion.** SwiGLU and the FP8 quantization of the W2 input are fused into one kernel. The weighted sum of the routed experts is deferred until it is merged with the shared expert. - **Tuning.** A Humming header overlay is added, and H20 tuning tables are loaded per role. ### mHC and FP8 GEMM **mHC.** The main problem with mHC was unstable results. - **Upstream.** On Hopper, upstream uses bf16x3 for mHC with more than 32 rows. On H20 the results change with the run and with batch size, and the error relative to fp64 is 5–10× larger. - **This branch.** We use tf32x3 split-K plus a sinkhorn written in TileLang. Results are deterministic, and from 2 rows up they do not change with batch size. - **Fusion.** - Each post is fused with the next sublayer's collapse. - With many rows, RMSNorm is fused in as well, and the result is bit-exact with FlashInfer's RMSNorm. **FP8 GEMM.** - Activations of block32 linear layers are quantized directly into the scale layout DeepGEMM expects. - Small-M GEMMs pick a swap-AB or split-K kernel from a tuning table. - wo_a stays in FP8, with inverse RoPE fused into the rounding kernel. - The DSpark draft uses an FP8 copy of the LM head. The target stays BF16 by default; quantizing the target is the lossy option. ## Decode: removing the work every GPU repeats On a single node, decode uses CP decode attention TP, and all 8 GPUs hold all decode rows. Upstream repeats the same per-row work on every GPU: - each GPU has only 8 attention heads, yet FlashMLA pads them to 64; - mHC and Engram compute all rows on every GPU; - all TP all-reduces go through FlashInfer. We split this work by row: - **Head↔row swap (from 96 rows).** Each GPU handles 1/8 of the rows, but computes attention with all 64 heads. On 8×H20-3e at 64 concurrent requests, a single FlashMLA call drops from 257 μs to 47 μs. - **TP-SP (from 64 rows).** Each GPU keeps only 1/8 of the residual stream. mHC, Engram and the DSpark capture compute only those rows. The result is bit-exact with the original path. Communication and scheduling: - **All-reduce.** TP all-reduce uses custom all-reduce v2. On 8×H20-3e at 64 concurrent requests, one call drops from 63 μs to 22 μs. - **Graph batch size.** CUDA graphs are captured at the real batch size. Upstream kept CP alignment, so a single session replayed the bs=4 graph and computed 24 rows instead of 6. - **FlashMLA tile schedule.** A cost model fitted on H20 picks the schedule. The scheduler is adapted from FlashMLA's `get_decoding_sched_meta` (MIT license). DSpark: - Draft rows are packed into a single row for FlashMLA. - Verify's greedy argmax and the draft's candidate selection run directly on the vocabulary shards. This skips the full gather of logits, and the result is the same as with the gather. - Draft preparation no longer copies lengths back to the host. That copy used to block the CPU for 2.8–2.9 ms per step. **PD decode role.** The decode role in PD uses attention DP, which needs a gather before MoE and a combine after it. - The gather moves from NCCL to an NVLink all-gather. - The combine changes from "all-reduce, then slice" to a direct reduce-scatter. - On an 8×H20 D at batch 256 (synthetic requests, 61440 input / 8192 output), this part of each step drops from 6.60 ms to 5.31 ms. ## Serving Commit 9 handles serving-layer issues. **DP dispatch for decode.** - **Upstream.** The DP controller refreshes its load snapshot every 20 ms. Each refresh drops requests that were sent but not yet received by the rank, so bursts keep flowing to ranks that are already full. - **This branch.** We count in-flight requests in the load and skip full ranks. - **Example.** With 128 requests sent at once to 8 ranks (16 max each), upstream assigns [25, 25, 13 × 6]; we now assign [16 × 8]. **Admission wait.** - DSpark has a rule that holds back prefill when fewer than 4 slots are free, so that requests can batch. - After a burst, the last few requests then idle through a whole decode round. At 64 concurrent requests, their TTFT is about 10 s. - Removing the rule outright makes TPOT worse and cuts throughput by 11%. So we cap this wait at 32 scheduling rounds. **SWA prefix reuse.** - Bounded replay writes late-layer rows only for the last window, so upstream backs off a whole window on every prefix match. - We record on the radix tree which ranges really have late-layer rows computed, and reuse the recorded parts directly. **HiCache.** Upstream does not allow `--hicache-size` for DeepSeek V4. Now the per-rank host cache can be set in GB. **PD failure handling:** - When prefill loses contact, decode no longer frees KV pages that may still be being written. It quarantines them and reclaims them after a late ACK arrives or after 300 s of lost contact. - When a prefill rank stops reporting, or its scheduler loop is stuck for more than 180 s, the bootstrap server's `/health` returns 503. Decode's heartbeat then marks it as lost. - When prefill gives up on a request before handoff, it tells decode the reason right away, so decode does not wait for a timeout. **These fixes apply to upstream as well:** - With CP + DSpark + bounded replay, the first request crashes because the tail gather has the wrong layout. - On SM90, hc-prenorm split-K races with WGMMA when the split count does not divide the K blocks. On H20 the relative error can reach 10–18%. - When cluster top-k's threshold bucket overflows, candidates are truncated arbitrarily. - PD handoff has several concurrent read/write races. ## EPD: separating encode, prefill and decode Upstream main does not support EPD deployment for V4.1 yet. Commit 10 completes this path: - E loads only the vision part, reading 2 of 48 weight shards. P and D do not load the vision tower, and prefill still uses CP. - Under CP, image features are merged into the full input before it is split. This fixes image Q&A, which used to fail on every request. - D asks E only for preprocessing metadata and no longer waits for image embeddings. - Encoders share an embedding cache through `/dev/shm`. A 503 caused by registration conflicts between multiple tokenizer workers is also fixed. ## Accuracy Single-run scores on 8×H20-3e, non-thinking mode (chat completions API), upstream vs this branch: | Benchmark | Upstream main | This branch | Difference (branch − upstream) | |---|---:|---:|---:| | MBPP+ | 81.45% | 81.38% | −0.07 | | RACE-middle | 96.03% | 96.52% | +0.49 | | RACE-high | 93.34% | 93.40% | +0.06 | | BFCL | 86.08% | 85.91% | −0.17 | | IFEval | 89.28% | 90.20% | +0.92 | | PIQA | 95.10% | 95.16% | +0.06 | | GSM8K | 97.06% | 96.76% | −0.30 | We also compared prefix-cache hits against cold computation: 3 lengths (8K / 40K / 100K) × 3 depths each. All 9 cases match. ## Reproduction **Code and model.** - The code is the `dsv41-flash-h20` branch of [github.com/antgroup/sglang](https://github.com/antgroup/sglang/tree/dsv41-flash-h20), head `6e6d5d9e13`. - The weights are [deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017) on Hugging Face. `/path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017` in the commands below is its local directory. **Runtime.** Use the upstream image for the baseline, `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-20261027-5884e4fe`. - The branch only changes `python/sglang` (plus tests and docs). It changes neither dependencies nor the precompiled sgl-kernel, so the image's CUDA, PyTorch, DeepGEMM and FlashInfer work as they are. - All results above were measured this way: dependencies from the image, code from this branch. Inside the image container: ```bash git clone -b dsv41-flash-h20 https://github.com/antgroup/sglang.git cd sglang && git checkout 6e6d5d9e13 export PYTHONPATH=$PWD/python ``` ### Single node (8×H20-3e) ```bash export SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_SM90=1 SGLANG_OPT_FP8_WO_A_GEMM=1 \ SGLANG_ENABLE_DSV41_ENGRAM_HOST_TABLE=1 SGLANG_DSV41_ENGRAM_HOST_TABLE_LAYOUT=per_rank \ SGLANG_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG='{"dtype": "float8e4m3"}' python3 -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path /path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 --served-model-name DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash \ --host 0.0.0.0 --trust-remote-code --language-model-only \ --tp-size 8 --enable-prefill-cp --cp-strategy interleave --enable-cp-decode-attn-tp \ --moe-runner-backend humming --enable-decoder-swa-bounded-replay --swa-full-tokens-ratio 0.05 \ --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 5 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.84 --max-running-requests 64 --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 64 \ --chunked-prefill-size 16384 --enable-cache-report --reasoning-parser auto --tool-call-parser auto ``` Apart from this branch's switch, the other environment variables are options that upstream main already has, off by default: - Engram tables in host memory, split per rank; - MoE input quantized to FP8 (W4A8); - the FP8 wo_a GEMM, which must be enabled explicitly on SM90. The upstream main baseline runs the SGLang bundled in the same image: - the same environment variables, but without `PYTHONPATH` and `SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_SM90`; - without `--enable-decoder-swa-bounded-replay`. ### EPD (2E3P1D) **Layout.** P and D each use one 8-GPU node. Each E process uses 1 GPU, and the 2 processes can share a node. **Routing.** Requests go through a PD router to P first, then to D. The router must use prefix-based cache affinity (like sglang-router's cache_aware policy); otherwise the cache hit rate across the P nodes drops noticeably. Environment variables shared by P and D: ```bash export PYTHONPATH=$PWD/python SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_SM90=1 SGLANG_DEFAULT_THINKING=1 \ SGLANG_ENABLE_DSV41_ENGRAM_HOST_TABLE=1 SGLANG_DSV41_ENGRAM_HOST_TABLE_LAYOUT=per_rank \ SGLANG_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG='{"dtype": "float8e4m3"}' SGLANG_VLM_CACHE_SIZE_MB=512 ``` **P** (one per node, 3 nodes in total): - `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 100` turns on SGLang HiCache L2, with 100 GB of host memory per rank for prefix KV. - In our internal deployment, P connects to Ant Group's internal KV cache system. The open-source version cannot integrate it, so the reproduction uses HiCache L2 in its place. - The cache hit rate and P's throughput vary with cache capacity. ```bash SGLANG_EMBEDDING_POOL_SIZE_MB=2048 python3 -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path /path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 --trust-remote-code --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8088 \ --tp-size 8 --enable-prefill-cp --cp-strategy interleave --enable-cp-decode-attn-tp \ --moe-runner-backend humming --enable-decoder-swa-bounded-replay --swa-full-tokens-ratio 0.05 \ --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 5 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.82 --max-running-requests 128 --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 128 \ --chunked-prefill-size 16384 --tokenizer-worker-num 4 \ --disaggregation-mode prefill --language-only --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 100 \ --enable-cache-report --reasoning-parser auto --tool-call-parser auto ``` **D** (1 node): ```bash SGLANG_EMBEDDING_POOL_SIZE_MB=0 SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_SM90_LOSSY=fp8_lm_head_target \ python3 -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path /path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 --trust-remote-code --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8089 \ --tp-size 8 --dp-size 8 --enable-dp-attention --enable-dp-lm-head \ --moe-runner-backend humming --swa-full-tokens-ratio 0.05 \ --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 5 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 --max-running-requests 256 --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 32 \ --chunked-prefill-size 16384 --tokenizer-worker-num 8 --load-balance-method total_tokens \ --disaggregation-mode decode --language-only --watchdog-timeout 1800 \ --enable-cache-report --reasoning-parser auto --tool-call-parser auto ``` **E** (one process per GPU): - Below is the first process. For the second, use another GPU and change `--port` and `--nccl-port` as well. - List the addresses of all P and D nodes in `--encoder-register-urls`. ```bash PYTHONPATH=$PWD/python SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_SM90=1 SGLANG_VLM_CACHE_SIZE_MB=512 \ SGLANG_ENCODER_MM_LOAD_WORKERS=8 REQUEST_TIMEOUT=180 CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 \ python3 -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path /path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 --trust-remote-code --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8090 --nccl-port 8190 \ --encoder-only --served-model-name DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash --mm-attention-backend fa3 \ --max-running-requests 64 --enable-mm-global-cache --mm-global-cache-backend shm \ --encoder-register-urls http://p1-host:8997 http://p2-host:8997 http://p3-host:8997 http://d-host:8997 ``` Configure the NCCL and Mooncake NIC settings for your cluster. ## Appendix: related community work Many changes in this branch build on existing community work, and many are aligned with work the community is pushing forward. The table lists related PRs and issues by commit, for cross-reference and for discussion when the changes are split up and upstreamed. The mapping comes from the "Community work" paragraph in each commit message. Numbers refer to sgl-project/sglang unless another repository is named. If we have missed anything or attributed something inaccurately, please tell us and we will correct it promptly. | Commit | Topic | Related community work | This branch's approach | |---|---|---|---| | 2 · fixes | CP tail-gather crash | `#45534`, `#45083` | Gathers directly in the tail layout | | | BF16 weight cache under CP decode TP | `#45083` | The cache is sliced and restored together with CP decode TP weights | | | SIGQUIT cleanup | `#39204`; `#45997`, `#40365` | Cleans up fully under uvicorn's multi-worker supervisor too | | | folded-accept buffer reuse | `#40919`, `#42812` | A copy event defers the next replay's write to the buffer | | | Abort during preparation | `#44449` | Re-sends the abort after the request is dispatched | | | top-k threshold-bucket overflow | `#43801`; `#37941`; issue `#36807` | Exact refinement of the cluster bucket | | | hc-prenorm split-K race | DeepGEMM `#448`; DeepGEMM issue `#449` | Until the kernel fix lands, the caller only picks splits that divide the K blocks | | | Empty residual in rejection sampling | `#42850` | Fixes the same issue in the Triton chain sampler | | | Sparse-prefill workspace growth | issue `#41076`; `#43726` | Frees the old allocation before growing | | 3 · mHC and MoE | mHC reproducibility | `#46523` | tf32x3, which also removes batch-size differences | | | mHC and norm fusion, statistics overlap | `#46088`; `#40891`, `#42985` | Folds the norm in from 1024 / 2048 rows | | | Humming version | `#46018` | Header overlay for 0.1.12 | | 4 · FP8 GEMM | MN-major scale | `#46838` | Writes UE8M0 MN-major scales directly, bit-exact with upstream | | | per-32 rounding before wo_a | `#45185` | The rounded result goes straight into the FP8 GEMM and fused kernels | | | Small-M GEMM | `#45166`; `#45828` | Picks swap-AB Gluon or split-K Triton from a tuning table | | | inverse RoPE fusion | `#43786`, `#44190` | Fused into the per-32 rounding before wo_a | | | grouped wo_a | `#46023` | Overlaps with its routing for grouped shapes | | 5 · cold start | mHC warm-up sharding | `#39363` | A deterministic rank stride instead of file locks | | | JIT warm-up and cache | issue `#32124` | Sampled warm-up plus manifest replay | | | Checkpoint page cache | `#40594`, `#45204` | Keeps the page cache for Engram prefetch | | 6 · indexer | Deterministic top-k ties | `#46522`, `#41893` | A separate JIT module keeps the smallest position | | | FP8 prefill scoring | `#45539` | Tiled and keys-major kernels also score compact candidates | | 7 · CP prefill | CP MoE communication | `#28639` | Copy-engine gather plus owner scatter-write and sum | | | Engram owner writes | `#46338`, `#45679` | On SM90 the owner writes CP rows directly | | | CP sparse prefill | `#36297`; `#38603` | CP-local queries use the gathered cache | | | CP prefill graphs | `#40333`; `#43089` | Lazy capture at the exact local row count; head and tail graph segments around the eager switching layers | | | Late-layer tail | `#46152` | Skips late layers while keeping the readers under CP | | 8 · decode | Draft metadata preparation | `#46891`, `#46897`, `#46777` | Already merged in main after the baseline; this part will be dropped at the next rebase | | | Engram read order | `#45879` | Skips sorting below 2¹⁷ (131072) ids | | | TP-local draft logits | `#44465` | Keeps the global token noise and tie rules | | | Sharded verify argmax | `#37106` | Grouped gather keeps argmax semantics | | | CUDA graph logical batch size | `#40543` | Relaxed further on the validated single-node (non-PD) roles | | | Per-row duplicate work in mix TP | `#45729`; `#43065` | Head swap plus TP-SP under TP decode | | 9 · serving and PD | DP load counting | `#44528` | Counts in-flight requests, skips full ranks, sorts by request count first | | | Admission wait | `#42280` | Keeps the wait, capped at 32 scheduling rounds | | | SWA coverage proof | `#46008` | Tree nodes carry a coverage proof | | | HiCache host pool | `#42554`, `#45173` | `--hicache-size` sizes each host pool by the device's FULL:SWA ratio | | | KV release after failure | issue `#44186` | Quarantined until a late ACK or confirmed loss of contact | | | Failed-room retention | `#44248`; issue `#39428` | A tombstone keeps the failure reason and acknowledges ABORT immediately | | | PD control thread | `#31966` | The control thread does not exit on message-handling errors | | 10 · EPD | V4.1 EPD enablement and throughput | `#43856` | Adds the shm cache, metadata requests and worker discovery | | | Image embeddings under CP | `#40219` | Merges first, then splits, and restores the token ids Engram and vision routing need | | | ViT RoPE | `#44451` | Half-split RoPE on FA3's strided QKV view | | | Embedding cache | `#45772`, `#35145` | shm file-backed shared cache | If we have missed anything or attributed something inaccurately, please tell us and we will correct it promptly. ## Acknowledgments - Thanks to the SGLang community, and especially to the authors of the PRs and issues in the table above, who found and started fixing many of these problems first. - Thanks to DeepSeek for the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 model and for open-sourcing [FlashMLA](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/FlashMLA) and [DeepGEMM](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM). This branch's decode tile scheduler is adapted from FlashMLA (MIT license; the notice is in `python/sglang/kernels/jit/THIRDPARTYNOTICES.txt`). - Thanks also to the Humming, Mooncake and TileLang projects. **About the writing:** the body of this article was drafted with AI assistance and the authors revised the wording. detail.body: # SGLang Optimizations for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on H20: 4–10× Faster Long-Input TTFT > Main authors: Hanlin Gao, Wengang Zheng, Yusong Gao, Yun Zhang > > This draft PR is a write-up, not a merge request. The code is the `dsv41-flash-h20` branch of this repository. The changes are meant to go upstream piece by piece. ## Introduction We run an agent workload whose requests average **about 170K input tokens** each, with short outputs. On H20 the first bottleneck for this traffic is prefill. **H20 has about one seventh of the compute of H100, but its NVLink is still 900 GB/s**, so it suits splitting one long request across several GPUs. The branch is based on SGLang upstream main (`5884e4fec6`, October 27, 2026; the same base throughout). It does three things: - **It spreads the prefill of a long input over 8 GPUs.** - **It removes the work that every GPU repeats during decode.** - **It puts every optimization behind one switch.** With the switch off, the code is upstream's, except for the commits that fix upstream bugs. This makes it easy to upstream the changes one at a time. **Results** - **Single node (8×H20-3e):** TTFT on long inputs is **4–10× faster** than upstream main. Decode throughput is **1.9–2.3×** that of upstream main. - **Cold start (8×H20, fresh container):** the time until the server can take requests drops from **31 minutes to 5.3 minutes**. - **Off-peak revenue per GPU-hour:** - On a 34-GPU minimal reproduction demo built from sampled internal business data (2E3P1D, a fixed 3:1 ratio), the two load levels give **¥26.8 (≈$4.0)** at about 50 token/s per user and **¥14.4 (≈$2.2)** at about 100 token/s per user. At the 100 TPS level, P is only about half used. - At our internal system's operating point, 100 token/s per user gives about **¥24.5 (≈$3.7)**. Revenue uses DeepSeek's official off-peak prices. USD figures use the CNY/USD ratio of DeepSeek's own price list (about 6.67). **Code and reproduction** - **Code:** [github.com/antgroup/sglang](https://github.com/antgroup/sglang/tree/dsv41-flash-h20), branch `dsv41-flash-h20` (head `6e6d5d9e13`), which is the head of this PR. - **Model:** [deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017) on Hugging Face. - **Reproducing:** - The single-node numbers can be reproduced with the commands in [Reproduction](#reproduction). - The demo's deployment commands are there too, but the sampled data is not public. - The open-source version cannot connect to Ant Group's internal KV cache system, so the reproduction uses SGLang HiCache L2 in its place. **At a glance: single node vs upstream main** (8×H20-3e, TP8 + prefill CP8 + DSpark) | Metric | Upstream main | This branch | Speedup | |---|---:|---:|---:| | TTFT (cold prefill), 4K input | 0.21 s | 0.09 s | 2.3× | | TTFT (cold prefill), 128K input | 6.9 s | 1.7 s | 4.0× | | TTFT (cold prefill), 512K input | 51.2 s | 7.5 s | 6.9× | | TTFT (cold prefill), 1M input | 163 s | 16.7 s | 9.8× | | Decode throughput, single session | 303 token/s | 583 token/s | 1.9× | | Decode throughput, 64 concurrent | 2.5K token/s | 5.8K token/s | 2.3× | | KV capacity | 20.6M tokens | 27.0M tokens | 1.3× | | Cold start to ready (fresh container, 8×H20 96 GB) | 31 min | 5.3 min | 5.9× | | TTFT of the first 128K request after cold start (same) | 364 s | 1.8 s | — | | GSM8K | 0.922 | 0.915 | — | **At a glance: throughput and revenue** (≈168K average input tokens; revenue per GPU-hour at DeepSeek off-peak prices) | | Output speed per user (p50) | Prefill per GPU (uncached / incl. cache hits) | Decode per GPU | Revenue per GPU-hour | Source | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---| | Demo, 50 TPS level | 51 token/s | 6.8K / 94K token/s | 1.5K token/s | ¥26.8 (≈$4.0) | Measured on the 34-GPU demo | | Demo, 100 TPS level | 95 token/s | 3.6K / 51K token/s | 829 token/s | ¥14.4 (≈$2.2) | Measured on the 34-GPU demo | | Internal system operating point | 100 token/s | 7.4K / 94K token/s | 930 token/s | ¥24.5 (≈$3.7) | Internal system operating point | **Versions** | Item | Value | |---|---| | Model | deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (Hugging Face) | | Baseline | SGLang upstream main, commit `5884e4fec6c0f4453940605896154f5fba4badd9` (merged 2026-10-27 00:07 UTC) | | Baseline image | `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-20261027-5884e4fe` (upstream nightly for that commit) | | This branch | [github.com/antgroup/sglang](https://github.com/antgroup/sglang/tree/dsv41-flash-h20), branch `dsv41-flash-h20` | | Branch head | `6e6d5d9e13915adb01db0856b15d6908eaaa2c48`, 10 commits on top of the baseline | | Scope of changes | Only `python/sglang`, plus tests and docs. Dependencies and sgl-kernel are unchanged, so the branch runs directly in the baseline image | | Measured | 2026-10-27 to 10-29 | | Hardware | Single node: 8×H20-3e (141 GB). Cold start and PD / EPD: 8×H20 (96 GB) nodes | To reproduce, use the upstream baseline image and this branch's code. Inside the image container: ```bash git clone -b dsv41-flash-h20 https://github.com/antgroup/sglang.git && cd sglang && git checkout 6e6d5d9e13 export PYTHONPATH=$PWD/python SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_SM90=1 python3 -m sglang.launch_server ... # full environment variables and arguments in "Reproduction" below ``` ## Results ### Single node: 8×H20-3e vs upstream main Both run TP8 + prefill CP8 + DSpark on the same machine. - The longer the input, the larger the gap: 4× faster at 128K and nearly 10× at 1M. - At 32 and 64 concurrent requests, decode throughput is more than 2.2× that of upstream main. | Metric | Upstream main | This branch | Speedup | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Cold-prefill TTFT, 4K input | 0.211 s | 0.092 s | 2.29× | | Cold-prefill TTFT, 64K input | 2.966 s | 0.857 s | 3.46× | | Cold-prefill TTFT, 128K input | 6.901 s | 1.724 s | 4.00× | | Cold-prefill TTFT, 256K input | 17.681 s | 3.522 s | 5.02× | | Cold-prefill TTFT, 512K input | 51.230 s | 7.476 s | 6.85× | | Cold-prefill TTFT, 1M (1016K) input | 163.386 s | 16.665 s | 9.80× | | Decode throughput, single session (4K in, 1K out) | 303.0 token/s | 583.0 token/s | 1.92× | | Decode throughput, 32 concurrent (total output) | 1982.8 token/s | 4460.7 token/s | 2.25× | | Decode throughput, 64 concurrent (total output) | 2518.1 token/s | 5773.9 token/s | 2.29× | | KV capacity | 20.56M tokens | 26.97M tokens | 1.31× | | Cold start to READY (8×H20 96 GB, fresh container) | 1850 s | 316 s | 5.9× | *Figure 1. This branch vs upstream main on a single node (8×H20-3e, TP8 + prefill CP8 + DSpark). The green numbers on the right are speedups.* ### Cold start: 31 minutes to 5.3 minutes Cold start does not change steady-state performance, but every new instance has to wait through it once. **Setup:** both sides start from a fresh container: the JIT cache is empty and the checkpoint is not in the page cache. **Result on 8×H20 (96 GB):** | | Time to READY | TTFT of the first 128K request after READY | |---|---:|---:| | Upstream main | 1850 s | 364 s | | This branch | 316 s | 1.8 s | *Figure 2. Cold start (8×H20, TP8 + prefill CP8 + DSpark, fresh container, checkpoint not in the page cache).* Upstream main spends its time in two places: - **CUDA graph capture takes 1395 s.** - Almost all of it goes to DeepGEMM precompiling every GEMM shape for every M from 1 to 32768. - After READY, the first 128K request hits two shapes that only appear in long prefills, and each triggers another round of compilation. So its TTFT is six minutes. - **Weight loading takes 340 s**, about 200 s of which is mHC warm-up compilation during loading. This branch changes three things: - It turns off full-M precompilation by default and warms up on sampled shapes. - It ships a JIT manifest with the code. While weights load, 32 processes compile the kernels in the manifest in parallel. - It keeps the page cache instead of dropping it. The result: - Weight loading takes 133 s and CUDA graph capture 86 s. - After READY, no new files appear in the JIT cache directory. - The first 128K request has about the same TTFT as steady state (1.74 s). Note: upstream provides `python3 -m sglang.compile_deep_gemm` to compile DeepGEMM ahead of time, which makes cold start much shorter. This comparison is a plain launch with no preparation. ### Minimal reproduction demo: 2E3P1D on 34 H20 GPUs This demo is a minimal reproduction. It checks the V4.1 PD / EPD path end to end and measures the per-GPU capacity of P and D. It does not represent how the real business is deployed or loaded. - **Traffic:** multi-turn sessions sampled from internal business data, about 47 minutes long, with an average input of about 168K tokens. The upstream implementation works, but carries a lot of extra overhead: - every per-layer row exchange goes through NCCL; - the compressor first gathers full hidden rows, then projects all rows on every GPU; - MoE output is all-reduced and then sliced; - under CP each layer also has about 4 ms of host overhead that does not depend on the row count, so for short inputs the host is the bottleneck. All of this communication now goes through NVLink symmetric memory: - **SWA KV and the compressor gathers** are issued by the copy engine before q_b and overlap with compute. - **The compressor** projects only its local rows and then gathers the projected results. The tail compressor goes from a 16384-row GEMM plus one full gather to a 2048-row GEMM plus one output gather. - **MoE.** From 2048 rows per GPU, the copy engine also pulls the MoE inputs. The weighted sum of the routed experts is written straight into each rank's symmetric buffer and then summed in FP32 in rank order. This removes the NCCL all-reduce and the slicing. - **Input embeddings and Engram lookups** are written directly from the shard owner to the target rank in the same way. ### Sparse prefill and late-layer skip **Sparse prefill.** Under CP, upstream sends query rows into the paged decode kernel. We switch back to `flash_mla_sparse_fwd`. On 8×H20, attention time for a cold 128K request drops from 222.8 ms to 199.1 ms. **Bounded replay.** The late-layer skip builds on upstream's bounded replay ([sgl-project/sglang#38798](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38798)). - V4.1 layers 21–39 reuse layer 20's KV, but each layer still has its own 128-token sliding window. - With bounded replay on, layer 20 and later layers compute only the last window of each prefill chunk, and the sliding window is truncated at that window's start. - So bounded replay is an approximation. The upstream docs say it is not numerically equivalent to a full prefill, and recommend turning it off for RL, where logprobs must match the trainer ([V4.1 cookbook](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/5884e4fec6c0f4453940605896154f5fba4badd9/docs/cookbook/autoregressive/DeepSeek/DeepSeek-V4_1.mdx)). - Upstream made it the default without CP in [sgl-project/sglang#44403](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/44403). - The PR's evaluations with it on and off are close: 97.71% for both on AIME 2026 with unlimited output, and 69.03% vs 68.14% on DeepSWE. - The PR also notes that single runs cannot prove accuracy equivalence. - This branch turns it on explicitly under CP8. Commit 2 fixes the crash when these options are combined. See [Accuracy](#accuracy) for the comparison. **Late-layer skip.** It builds on bounded replay. - Suppose that after a chunk, every request still has at least one window left unfilled. That window will be overwritten by a later chunk, so computing it is wasted: nothing reads it. - In that case the whole chunk stops at layer 20 (of 40). Under CP, the row layout that logits and DSpark need is still kept. The result is bit-exact with bounded replay itself. - The scheduler helps guarantee that every late-layer value that is read comes from a full forward pass: - a continuation chunk that falls inside the last window must contain the whole window; - a request that hits the radix cache must re-prefill its last window. ### Prefill CUDA graphs The ≈4 ms per-layer host overhead is removed with CUDA graphs. - **Capture.** Graphs are captured lazily, at the exact local row count, with no padding. A row count is captured the second time it appears. Each segment keeps at most 32 graphs, evicted LRU. - **What stays eager.** The CP KV gather, the indexer and the attention core still run eagerly. - **Failure handling.** After capture, and before the custom all-reduce graph inputs are registered, all ranks vote. If any rank failed to capture, all ranks discard the capture together and fall back to eager. ### Sparse-attention indexer In V4.1's ratio-1/2 layers, an indexer first picks the top-k KV positions for each query, and then sparse attention runs on them. Upstream's prefill indexer is in torch: it dequantizes the index keys to BF16, runs an einsum, then calls `torch.topk`. **Prefill.** - We unpack each request's FP4 keys once, convert them to E4M3 and score them with FP8 tensor cores. - Once the scoring size reaches 2M, H20 switches to a keys-major Gluon kernel. - Top-k uses top-k v2. On ties it always keeps the earlier position, so the result no longer depends on the order of atomics. - Scores match the torch path within tolerance. **Decode and verify.** - FP4 keys are scored straight from the request table. - Several verify rows of the same request share the decoded key tiles. - When there are enough candidate windows, consumer layers score only the candidate blocks instead of scanning the whole context. ### MoE: Humming W4A8 V4.1-Flash stores its routed-expert weights in FP4 (MXFP4), but H20 is a Hopper GPU without FP4 tensor cores. This part uses Humming ([github.com/vllm-project/humming](https://github.com/vllm-project/humming)), **open-sourced by Ant Group**, a JIT-compiled quantized GEMM library. - **How it works.** Humming converts the FP4 weights to FP8 inside the kernel, with the weights' E8M0 scales folded into the operands ahead of time. It then feeds them, together with FP8 activations, into the FP8 tensor cores (W4A8). - **Why it helps.** The weights stay 4-bit in memory, so less data is read, and the compute still runs at FP8 speed. - **Adoption.** SGLang already integrates it as an MoE backend ([sgl-project/sglang#23754](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/23754)). FlashInfer's recent MXFP4×FP8 MoE path for Hopper follows Humming's weight preprocessing and dequantization method (`flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#3738`). Humming is very efficient on H20. We once profiled a cold 128K prefill (TP4 + CP4): - the two routed-expert GEMMs took more than a third of GPU time; - from measured kernel times and shapes, w13 and w2 reached 84% and 83% of FP8 dense peak. This branch changes how Humming is used: - **Stream-K is off.** It accumulates K slices in arrival order, so the first token of a short input could vary from run to run. - **Less padding.** Per-rank weight padding shrinks from 256/128 to 64/64. Under TP8, w13's N drops from 768 to 576. - **Fusion.** SwiGLU and the FP8 quantization of the W2 input are fused into one kernel. The weighted sum of the routed experts is deferred until it is merged with the shared expert. - **Tuning.** A Humming header overlay is added, and H20 tuning tables are loaded per role. ### mHC and FP8 GEMM **mHC.** The main problem with mHC was unstable results. - **Upstream.** On Hopper, upstream uses bf16x3 for mHC with more than 32 rows. On H20 the results change with the run and with batch size, and the error relative to fp64 is 5–10× larger. - **This branch.** We use tf32x3 split-K plus a sinkhorn written in TileLang. Results are deterministic, and from 2 rows up they do not change with batch size. - **Fusion.** - Each post is fused with the next sublayer's collapse. - With many rows, RMSNorm is fused in as well, and the result is bit-exact with FlashInfer's RMSNorm. **FP8 GEMM.** - Activations of block32 linear layers are quantized directly into the scale layout DeepGEMM expects. - Small-M GEMMs pick a swap-AB or split-K kernel from a tuning table. - wo_a stays in FP8, with inverse RoPE fused into the rounding kernel. - The DSpark draft uses an FP8 copy of the LM head. The target stays BF16 by default; quantizing the target is the lossy option. ## Decode: removing the work every GPU repeats On a single node, decode uses CP decode attention TP, and all 8 GPUs hold all decode rows. Upstream repeats the same per-row work on every GPU: - each GPU has only 8 attention heads, yet FlashMLA pads them to 64; - mHC and Engram compute all rows on every GPU; - all TP all-reduces go through FlashInfer. We split this work by row: - **Head↔row swap (from 96 rows).** Each GPU handles 1/8 of the rows, but computes attention with all 64 heads. On 8×H20-3e at 64 concurrent requests, a single FlashMLA call drops from 257 μs to 47 μs. - **TP-SP (from 64 rows).** Each GPU keeps only 1/8 of the residual stream. mHC, Engram and the DSpark capture compute only those rows. The result is bit-exact with the original path. Communication and scheduling: - **All-reduce.** TP all-reduce uses custom all-reduce v2. On 8×H20-3e at 64 concurrent requests, one call drops from 63 μs to 22 μs. - **Graph batch size.** CUDA graphs are captured at the real batch size. Upstream kept CP alignment, so a single session replayed the bs=4 graph and computed 24 rows instead of 6. - **FlashMLA tile schedule.** A cost model fitted on H20 picks the schedule. The scheduler is adapted from FlashMLA's `get_decoding_sched_meta` (MIT license). DSpark: - Draft rows are packed into a single row for FlashMLA. - Verify's greedy argmax and the draft's candidate selection run directly on the vocabulary shards. This skips the full gather of logits, and the result is the same as with the gather. - Draft preparation no longer copies lengths back to the host. That copy used to block the CPU for 2.8–2.9 ms per step. **PD decode role.** The decode role in PD uses attention DP, which needs a gather before MoE and a combine after it. - The gather moves from NCCL to an NVLink all-gather. - The combine changes from "all-reduce, then slice" to a direct reduce-scatter. - On an 8×H20 D at batch 256 (synthetic requests, 61440 input / 8192 output), this part of each step drops from 6.60 ms to 5.31 ms. ## Serving Commit 9 handles serving-layer issues. **DP dispatch for decode.** - **Upstream.** The DP controller refreshes its load snapshot every 20 ms. Each refresh drops requests that were sent but not yet received by the rank, so bursts keep flowing to ranks that are already full. - **This branch.** We count in-flight requests in the load and skip full ranks. - **Example.** With 128 requests sent at once to 8 ranks (16 max each), upstream assigns [25, 25, 13 × 6]; we now assign [16 × 8]. **Admission wait.** - DSpark has a rule that holds back prefill when fewer than 4 slots are free, so that requests can batch. - After a burst, the last few requests then idle through a whole decode round. At 64 concurrent requests, their TTFT is about 10 s. - Removing the rule outright makes TPOT worse and cuts throughput by 11%. So we cap this wait at 32 scheduling rounds. **SWA prefix reuse.** - Bounded replay writes late-layer rows only for the last window, so upstream backs off a whole window on every prefix match. - We record on the radix tree which ranges really have late-layer rows computed, and reuse the recorded parts directly. **HiCache.** Upstream does not allow `--hicache-size` for DeepSeek V4. Now the per-rank host cache can be set in GB. **PD failure handling:** - When prefill loses contact, decode no longer frees KV pages that may still be being written. It quarantines them and reclaims them after a late ACK arrives or after 300 s of lost contact. - When a prefill rank stops reporting, or its scheduler loop is stuck for more than 180 s, the bootstrap server's `/health` returns 503. Decode's heartbeat then marks it as lost. - When prefill gives up on a request before handoff, it tells decode the reason right away, so decode does not wait for a timeout. **These fixes apply to upstream as well:** - With CP + DSpark + bounded replay, the first request crashes because the tail gather has the wrong layout. - On SM90, hc-prenorm split-K races with WGMMA when the split count does not divide the K blocks. On H20 the relative error can reach 10–18%. - When cluster top-k's threshold bucket overflows, candidates are truncated arbitrarily. - PD handoff has several concurrent read/write races. ## EPD: separating encode, prefill and decode Upstream main does not support EPD deployment for V4.1 yet. Commit 10 completes this path: - E loads only the vision part, reading 2 of 48 weight shards. P and D do not load the vision tower, and prefill still uses CP. - Under CP, image features are merged into the full input before it is split. This fixes image Q&A, which used to fail on every request. - D asks E only for preprocessing metadata and no longer waits for image embeddings. - Encoders share an embedding cache through `/dev/shm`. A 503 caused by registration conflicts between multiple tokenizer workers is also fixed. ## Accuracy Single-run scores on 8×H20-3e, non-thinking mode (chat completions API), upstream vs this branch: | Benchmark | Upstream main | This branch | Difference (branch − upstream) | |---|---:|---:|---:| | MBPP+ | 81.45% | 81.38% | −0.07 | | RACE-middle | 96.03% | 96.52% | +0.49 | | RACE-high | 93.34% | 93.40% | +0.06 | | BFCL | 86.08% | 85.91% | −0.17 | | IFEval | 89.28% | 90.20% | +0.92 | | PIQA | 95.10% | 95.16% | +0.06 | | GSM8K | 97.06% | 96.76% | −0.30 | We also compared prefix-cache hits against cold computation: 3 lengths (8K / 40K / 100K) × 3 depths each. The upstream main baseline runs the SGLang bundled in the same image: - the same environment variables, but without `PYTHONPATH` and `SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_SM90`; - without `--enable-decoder-swa-bounded-replay`. ### EPD (2E3P1D) **Layout.** P and D each use one 8-GPU node. Each E process uses 1 GPU, and the 2 processes can share a node. **Routing.** Requests go through a PD router to P first, then to D. The router must use prefix-based cache affinity (like sglang-router's cache_aware policy); otherwise the cache hit rate across the P nodes drops noticeably. Environment variables shared by P and D: ```bash export PYTHONPATH=$PWD/python SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_SM90=1 SGLANG_DEFAULT_THINKING=1 \ SGLANG_ENABLE_DSV41_ENGRAM_HOST_TABLE=1 SGLANG_DSV41_ENGRAM_HOST_TABLE_LAYOUT=per_rank \ SGLANG_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG='{"dtype": "float8e4m3"}' SGLANG_VLM_CACHE_SIZE_MB=512 ``` **P** (one per node, 3 nodes in total): - `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 100` turns on SGLang HiCache L2, with 100 GB of host memory per rank for prefix KV. - In our internal deployment, P connects to Ant Group's internal KV cache system. The open-source version cannot integrate it, so the reproduction uses HiCache L2 in its place. - The cache hit rate and P's throughput vary with cache capacity. ```bash SGLANG_EMBEDDING_POOL_SIZE_MB=2048 python3 -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path /path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 --trust-remote-code --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8088 \ --tp-size 8 --enable-prefill-cp --cp-strategy interleave --enable-cp-decode-attn-tp \ --moe-runner-backend humming --enable-decoder-swa-bounded-replay --swa-full-tokens-ratio 0.05 \ --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 5 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.82 --max-running-requests 128 --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 128 \ --chunked-prefill-size 16384 --tokenizer-worker-num 4 \ --disaggregation-mode prefill --language-only --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 100 \ --enable-cache-report --reasoning-parser auto --tool-call-parser auto ``` **D** (1 node): ```bash SGLANG_EMBEDDING_POOL_SIZE_MB=0 SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_SM90_LOSSY=fp8_lm_head_target \ python3 -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path /path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 --trust-remote-code --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8089 \ --tp-size 8 --dp-size 8 --enable-dp-attention --enable-dp-lm-head \ --moe-runner-backend humming --swa-full-tokens-ratio 0.05 \ --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 5 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 --max-running-requests 256 --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 32 \ --chunked-prefill-size 16384 --tokenizer-worker-num 8 --load-balance-method total_tokens \ --disaggregation-mode decode --language-only --watchdog-timeout 1800 \ --enable-cache-report --reasoning-parser auto --tool-call-parser auto ``` **E** (one process per GPU): - Below is the first process. For the second, use another GPU and change `--port` and `--nccl-port` as well. - List the addresses of all P and D nodes in `--encoder-register-urls`. ```bash PYTHONPATH=$PWD/python SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_SM90=1 SGLANG_VLM_CACHE_SIZE_MB=512 \ SGLANG_ENCODER_MM_LOAD_WORKERS=8 REQUEST_TIMEOUT=180 CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 \ python3 -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path /path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 --trust-remote-code --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8090 --nccl-port 8190 \ --encoder-only --served-model-name DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash --mm-attention-backend fa3 \ --max-running-requests 64 --enable-mm-global-cache --mm-global-cache-backend shm \ --encoder-register-urls http://p1-host:8997 http://p2-host:8997 http://p3-host:8997 http://d-host:8997 ``` Configure the NCCL and Mooncake NIC settings for your cluster. ## Appendix: related community work Many changes in this branch build on existing community work, and many are aligned with work the community is pushing forward. The table lists related PRs and issues by commit, for cross-reference and for discussion when the changes are split up and upstreamed. +"""Clamped SwiGLU with per-row FP8 quantization in one pass over the gate/up rows.
+
+Bitwise ``act_and_mul_triton(swiglu_limit=...)`` (BF16 output) followed by Humming's
+dynamic float8e4m3 input quant with one float32 scale per row
+(``humming.ops.input.quant_input``, group_size 0); the expressions below are copied
+from both kernels, so the same Triton build rounds them identically.
+"""
+
+import torch
+import triton
+import triton.language as tl
+
+from sglang.kernels.ops.moe.fused_moe_triton_kernels import _apply_activation
+
+
+@triton.jit
+def _swiglu(
+    gate_up_ptr,
+    row,
+    row_ok,
+    stride,
+    col0,
+    N: tl.constexpr,
+    BLOCK: tl.constexpr,
+    SWIGLU_LIMIT: tl.constexpr,
+):
+    cols = col0 + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
+    mask = row_ok[:, None] & (cols < N)[None, :]
+    gate_ptrs = gate_up_ptr + row[:, None] * stride + cols[None, :]
+    gate = tl.load(gate_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0.0)
+    up = tl.load(gate_ptrs + N, mask=mask, other=0.0)
+    # act_and_mul_kernel, HAS_SWIGLU_LIMIT, silu.
+    gate = tl.minimum(gate, SWIGLU_LIMIT)
+    up = tl.maximum(tl.minimum(up, SWIGLU_LIMIT), -SWIGLU_LIMIT)
+    act = _apply_activation(gate, "silu").to(tl.bfloat16)
+    # Padding lanes hold +0 and cannot raise the row's absmax.
+    return (act * up).to(tl.bfloat16).to(tl.float32), cols, mask
+
+
+@triton.jit
+def _silu_mul_fp8_row_quant_kernel(
+    gate_up_ptr,
+    q_ptr,
+    scale_ptr,
+    rows,
+    stride_gate_up,
+    stride_q,
+    N: tl.constexpr,
+    BLOCK_A: tl.constexpr,
+    BLOCK_B: tl.constexpr,
+    ROWS: tl.constexpr,
+    SWIGLU_LIMIT: tl.constexpr,
+):
+    # Each row is two column tiles, [0, BLOCK_A) and [BLOCK_A, N) padded to BLOCK_B,
+    # so a row of 576 runs 512 + 64 lanes instead of 1024.
+    row = tl.program_id(0).to(tl.int64) * ROWS + tl.arange(0, ROWS)
+    row_ok = row < rows
+    a, cols_a, mask_a = _swiglu(
+        gate_up_ptr, row, row_ok, stride_gate_up, 0, N, BLOCK_A, SWIGLU_LIMIT
+    )
+    absmax = tl.max(tl.abs(a), axis=1)
+    if BLOCK_B > 0:
+        b, cols_b, mask_b = _swiglu(
+            gate_up_ptr, row, row_ok, stride_gate_up, BLOCK_A, N, BLOCK_B, SWIGLU_LIMIT
+        )
+        absmax = tl.maximum(absmax, tl.max(tl.abs(b), axis=1))
+    # humming _quant_tensor_kernel: float8e4m3, dynamic, float32 scale.
+    absmax = tl.maximum(absmax, 1e-30)
+    scale = absmax / 448
+    inv_scale = 1 / scale
+    q_row = q_ptr + row[:, None] * stride_q
+    q_a = (a * inv_scale[:, None]).to(tl.float8e4nv)
+    tl.store(q_row + cols_a[None, :], q_a, mask=mask_a)
+    if BLOCK_B > 0:
+        q_b = (b * inv_scale[:, None]).to(tl.float8e4nv)
+        tl.store(q_row + cols_b[None, :], q_b, mask=mask_b)
+    tl.store(scale_ptr + row, scale, mask=row_ok)
+
+
+def silu_mul_fp8_row_quant(
+    gate_up: torch.Tensor,
+    *,
+    swiglu_limit: float,
+    out: torch.Tensor,
+) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
+    """gate_up [M, 2N] bf16 (gate | up) -> (out [M, N] float8_e4m3fn, scale [M, 1]
+    float32), the down-projection input and its per-row scale."""
+    assert gate_up.dtype == torch.bfloat16 and gate_up.stride(-1) == 1
+    rows, two_n = gate_up.shape
+    n = two_n // 2
+    assert out.shape == (rows, n) and out.dtype == torch.float8_e4m3fn
+    assert out.stride(-1) == 1
+    scale = torch.empty((rows, 1), dtype=torch.float32, device=gate_up.device)
+    if rows == 0:
+        return out, scale
+    block_a = 1 << (n.bit_length() - 1)
+    block_b = triton.next_power_of_2(n - block_a) if n > block_a else 0
+    # Measured on H20-3e at 98304 x 576: 4 rows x 4 warps 118 us; 1-16 rows and
+    # 1-8 warps are no faster (SiLU's exp and divide bound it, not HBM).
+    rows_per_program = 4
+    _silu_mul_fp8_row_quant_kernel[(triton.cdiv(rows, rows_per_program),)](
+        gate_up,
+        out,
+        scale,
+        rows,
+        gate_up.stride(0),
+        out.stride(0),
+        N=n,
+        BLOCK_A=block_a,
+        BLOCK_B=block_b,
+        ROWS=rows_per_program,
+        SWIGLU_LIMIT=float(swiglu_limit),
+        num_warps=4,
+    )
+    return out, scale

+"""Packed vision SwiGLU with the eager SiLU intermediate rounding."""
+
+import torch
+import triton
+import triton.language as tl
+from triton.language.extra import libdevice
+
+
+@triton.jit(do_not_specialize=["numel"])
+def _vision_swiglu(X, Y, numel, D: tl.constexpr, B: tl.constexpr):
+    i = tl.program_id(0) * B + tl.arange(0, B)
+    mask = i < numel
+    ix = (i // D) * (2 * D) + i % D
+    gate = tl.load(X + ix, mask, 0).to(tl.float32)
+    up = tl.load(X + ix + D, mask, 0).to(tl.float32)
+    # Aten silu computes x / (1 + exp(-x)) and stores it in the input dtype;
+    # keep that rounding point and the separate rounding of the multiply.
+    activated = libdevice.div_rn(gate, 1.0 + libdevice.exp(-gate))
+    activated = activated.to(X.dtype.element_ty).to(tl.float32)
+    tl.store(Y + i, activated * up, mask)
+
+
+def vision_swiglu(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
+    """Return ``silu(x[:, :D]) * x[:, D:]`` for a contiguous [rows, 2 * D] input.
+
+    Bitwise ``F.silu(gate) * up``: SiLU is rounded to the input dtype before
+    the multiply, as the two eager kernels do.
+    """
+    if not (
+        x.is_cuda
+        and x.ndim == 2
+        and x.is_contiguous()
+        and x.dtype in (torch.bfloat16, torch.float32)
+        and x.shape[-1] % 2 == 0
+    ):
+        raise ValueError("Unsupported vision SwiGLU layout/dtype")
+    out = torch.empty((x.shape[0], x.shape[1] // 2), device=x.device, dtype=x.dtype)
+    if out.numel():
+        with torch.cuda.device(x.device):
+            _vision_swiglu[(triton.cdiv(out.numel(), 512),)](
+                x, out, out.numel(), out.shape[-1], 512, enable_fp_fusion=False
+            )
+    return out
